title: bread, wine, "do this in memory of me"
hook: bread, wine, "do this in memory of me"

segments.voice: Yesterday, scene two: the room turning around to shake hands before going to the table. Your line was: turn to the stranger. Who did you greet? Day five.

Think of a meal your family makes on one day of the year. Somebody's stuffing. A soup nobody else gets right. When you eat it, you're not only eating. You're back at a table with people who might not be alive anymore. The taste carries the memory in. Now picture a room in Jerusalem, the night before Jesus died. A festival meal, the Passover, itself a meal of memory. He takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, hands it around, and says something nobody at that table had heard before. Today, the last scene of the Mass, and the words it's built on.
screen: `A MEAL THAT CARRIES PEOPLE BACK.` → `A ROOM IN JERUSALEM.` → `BREAD, BROKEN AND SHARED.`

segments.voice: Luke's Gospel tells it this way, in the Douay-Rheims Bible. Jesus takes the bread, and says: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me." Then the cup, which he calls the new covenant in his blood. At every Catholic Mass, the priest says those words again over bread and wine at the altar. It's the center of the whole service, the moment everything has been walking toward. Here's the word underneath commemoration. In Greek it's anamnesis. It doesn't mean remembering the way you remember a phone number. It means making something present by remembering it. The Passover already worked that way. At that meal, Jewish families told the story of leaving Egypt as if they themselves had walked out. Catholics say the Mass works like that, and more. They believe that at those words, the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ, and that the one sacrifice of the cross is made present again, not repeated. That's a big claim, and we'll come back to it on day seventeen. Christians don't all agree about what happens. Orthodox Christians also speak of a real presence. Many Protestants understand the meal mainly as a memorial and a sign. What they all share is the table, and the command: do this. Then comes the ending. People come forward and receive communion, and the Mass closes with a blessing and a sending out. Go, you are sent. Remember day three? The name of the Mass is in that sending. The story, the peace, the table, and then the door.
screen: `THIS IS MY BODY.` · `ANAMNESIS — MEMORY THAT MAKES PRESENT.` · `CHRISTIANS DON'T ALL AGREE.` · `THE TABLE, THEN THE DOOR.` · then, large: `A MEAL IS A MEMORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Three breaths, with the bell. Think of one meal that carries someone for you. A dish, a table, a person who made it. On the first breath, see the table. On the second, see who's there. On the third, taste it. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If you don't, just let them be present for a moment.
The Mass, scene three. The table: bread and wine, the words of the Last Supper, communion, and then being sent out. Fifth word.
Your line: a meal is a memory. Today, at one meal, think of who taught you to eat it, grow it or make it. Day five.

screen: `DAY 5 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A TEENAGE GIRL SAYS YES.`

fork.setup: you're at the table the night before Jesus dies. he breaks the bread and hands it around. what does he ask you to do?
options: do this in memory of him.
fork.reveal: "do this for a commemoration of me." Christians have done it ever since, every Sunday and in many places every day.

original.note: Greek: remembrance, commemoration. a memory that makes something present again.

trapdoor: what you thought: church people eat a little bread to remember Jesus.
what it means: Catholics believe the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood, and the cross is made present again.
what a scholar hears: anamnesis, remembrance as re-presentation, rooted in the Passover, where each generation tells the exodus as its own.
